slides.0.title: Principles of food and wine pairing
slides.0.subtitle: Pairing is not a list to memorise but an understanding of how tastes interact
slides.1.title: Food elements that make wine taste worse
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Sweetness
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Sweetness in food makes wine seem more acidic, bitter and astringent, with less fruit and sweetness; the rule is that the wine should be at least as sweet as the food (dessert with sweet wine)
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Umami
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Umami in mushrooms, aged cheese and soy sauce also makes wine seem more bitter, astringent and acidic; a little salt or acid in the dish helps
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Chilli heat and bitterness
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Chilli heat amplifies alcohol burn and bitterness, so it suits low-alcohol, low-tannin wines with a touch of sweetness (off-dry Riesling with spicy food); bitterness in food increases bitterness in wine
slides.1.content: Sweetness, umami, heat and bitterness make wine “harder”: choose softer, sweeter or lower-alcohol wines.
slides.2.title: Elements that flatter wine, and classic pairings
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Salt and acid
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Salt and acid in food make wine seem softer, fruitier and fuller; acidic food needs a wine with enough acidity, or the wine tastes flat
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Fat and protein
slides.2.highlights.1.content: High acidity cuts through richness (Champagne with fried food); tannic reds suit red meat rich in protein and fat, as tannin binds with protein and feels softer
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Why classic pairings work
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Sancerre with goat’s cheese (acid with acid, salt), Sauternes with blue cheese (sweet with salt), Barolo with beef (tannin with protein). Explaining why matters more than memorising the pairing
slides.2.content: CMS service exams often ask you to recommend a wine and explain why: use these principles for the why.
slides.3.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
What is the basic rule for pairing wine with dessert?
A. Sweetness does not matter
B. The wine should be at least as sweet as the food
C. Choose the driest wine
D. Choose the most tannic wine
Otherwise the wine tastes sour and bitter.
Which wine suits spicy food best?
A. A rich red aged in new oak
B. A dry fortified Sherry
C. Low alcohol, low tannin, a touch of sweetness
D. High alcohol and high tannin
Heat amplifies alcohol and bitterness.
Why does Champagne suit fried food?
A. Champagne is very sweet
B. Champagne is very tannic
C. Champagne is very alcoholic
D. High acidity and bubbles cut through the richness
Acid against fat is a classic balance.
Which principle underlies Sauternes with blue cheese?
A. Sweet with salty
B. Tannin with protein
C. Acid with acid
D. Heat with sweetness
Salt makes the sweet wine seem more balanced.
